### TAG-215: Value-to-place reification for token-identity dispatch

**Status:** ⬜ Not started

## Software Notes

Two separable findings here, and the second one is unrelated to bundling entirely — a real, previously-latent emitter bug that `bus` happens to be the first example to trip.

Runtime: [TAG-213](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-213/runtimeparser-bare-name-bundle-aliasing-at-invocation-boundaries) slice 2a itself worked — this is a new, deeper gap

The error moved from `BundleInvocationNotSupported` to `ValueKeyedInvocationNotSupported`. That's confirmation `bindArgument` is doing its job correctly: the group `{$Q1 $Q2 $Q3 $Q4}` bound successfully against `fanin`'s declared group port. The failure is now coming from somewhere else — and I think it's more fundamental than either of us had framed it.

Look at `fanin`'s actual dispatch mechanism:

```
$select( ) : A[out<$in1>]
             B[out<$in2>]
             C[out<$in3>]
             D[out<$in4>]
```

This compiles, via the "fill-shaped children" path, into rules like `inputs=["A"], dest="out", copy_from("in1")`. That rule only fires when a place literally named `"A"` is valid. The *only* thing that ever makes that happen today is `Testbench`'s seeding — `env.seed(stream.port, tok); env.seed(tok, tok);` — which asserts a place named after whatever token arrives, by design, as that code's own comment says: *"standing in for whatever upstream mechanism would normally assert them from A/B."* It's a test-harness convenience, not a real runtime rule.

Inside `inlineInvocation`, nothing recreates that. `bus` passes `$selector_out`'s *value* (say `"A"`) into `fanin`'s `select` port via ordinary binding — but ordinary binding only makes the place `select` valid with value `"A"`; it never separately asserts a place *named* `"A"`. So `checkInvocable` correctly sees that `"A"` is neither a source port nor produced by any rule, and refuses rather than stalling silently. The guard is doing exactly its job — it's just revealing that the mechanism it's protecting against is broader than its own comment says.

**I think this is the same underlying gap as the FULLADD-chaining problem, not a second one.** What both actually need is a real rule — not a test-harness seeding hack — for "a place holding value `V` makes place `V` valid too." For FULLADD, that would be what lets a chained carry-out's value (`M`) become available as place `M` for a downstream joint match that references `M`. For `fanin`, it's exactly what select-dispatch needs. If that's right, it's one feature, not two, and it would mean `Testbench`'s current seeding is standing in for something that should actually exist as a runtime rule.

I'm not confident enough to just build that, though — it's a real design question, not a patch. In particular: does this apply to *every* place in the network, or only boundary/source ports? A blanket rule risks real collisions (two unrelated places both happening to hold `"1"` at some point would both try to assert place `"1"`). This is exactly the kind of thing worth checking against the book before implementing, the same way we held off on bare-name bundle aliasing. I'd file this as its own ticket — something like "value-to-place reification for token-identity dispatch" — and note it as likely the real blocker behind both `FULLADD` chaining and `fanin`/`fanout` invocation, rather than two separate deferred items.

**No regressions**, for what it's worth — `AND3`, `fulladd_gates`, [TAG-177](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-177/example-1226-pure-value-expression-of-boolean-full-adder), [TAG-181](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-181/example-1211-controlled-fan-out-expression), [TAG-198](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-198/example-1225-pure-value-expression), [TAG-143](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-143/example-122-expressing-a-single-return-to-place-of-invocation) are all still green, so slice 2a's binding change is safe on its own.

## GHDL: a genuine forward-reference bug in the emitter, unrelated to bundling

```
unit "fanin" not found in library "work"
```

This isn't about [TAG-213](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-213/runtimeparser-bare-name-bundle-aliasing-at-invocation-boundaries) Slice 2 at all. Look at your source order: `bus` is defined *before* `fanin`/`fanout`. The emitter writes each definition's VHDL block in `net.definitions` order, so `bus`'s architecture — which does `entity work.fanin port map (...)` — gets analyzed by `ghdl -a` *before* `fanin`'s own `entity`/`architecture` block appears later in the same file. Direct entity instantiation (as opposed to component instantiation with deferred binding) needs the target already analyzed into the library at that point. `AND3` and the `fulladd_gates` example only worked because you happened to write the callee (`AND`, `NOT`/`AND`/`OR`) before the caller in those files — not because the emitter guarantees correct ordering. Nothing in the language should require writing definitions in dependency order, so this would bite the next example that happens to define its top-level entry point first, the more natural way to write one.

The right fix is a topological sort of `net.definitions` before emission — callees always written before any caller that invokes them. I don't want to write that patch blind, though: I don't know what currently drives the iteration over `net.definitions` for emission (it isn't in either file from last time). Could you paste that — whatever calls `writeDefinition`/`writeDefinitionInNetwork` across the whole network, likely in `export.zig` or wherever `exportToString`'s real (non-test) counterpart lives?

One more data point in the same run, worth noting as confirmation rather than concern: [TAG-138](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-138/example-1240-the-invocation-expression-of-the-greatest-common-divisor) moved from `parse: ok` / GHDL-fail to `parse: FAIL`. That's `validate.zig`'s new `UndefinedInvocation` check doing exactly what we predicted a few turns back — TAG-138's `gcd_ltsteer`/`gcd_dualfanin`/`gcd_ms_mod` were never actually defined in-file, so it's now caught at parse time instead of surfacing as a confusing GHDL "unit not found" error. Expected, and arguably a better failure mode than before.

Good question, and my phrasing was unclear in a way that's worth fixing before we go further. You're right that two unrelated places holding the same value is completely fine — that happens constantly and is never a problem (two inputs both holding `"1"` is normal, not a conflict). That's not what I meant, and "assert place 'A'" was a sloppy way to say what I actually meant, so let me redo it precisely.

**What the dispatch mechanism actually needs isn't "a place with some name" — it's a place with one *exact* name, used purely as a yes/no flag, not as a value holder.** `fanin`'s rule `inputs=["A"], dest="out", copy_from("in1")` doesn't check "does select's value equal the string A" by comparing values — it checks `env.isValid("A")`, i.e., "does a place *literally named* `A` currently exist and hold anything at all." The actual value stored in that place is irrelevant; its mere validity is the signal. That's a specific implementation choice (token-identity-as-dispatch) in this runtime, not something inherent to the language — Fant's dispatch tables could equally be read as "match select's *value* against each branch's name," which is a different mechanism (and one we already have working elsewhere, more on that below).

**The real risk isn't values colliding — it's two *unrelated* synthesized places colliding on the same name, in a shared namespace.** Here's the concrete case: suppose `bus` invokes `fanin` twice (unlikely for `bus` specifically, but easy to imagine elsewhere), and separately some other part of the network has its own place that happens to hold the symbol `"A"` for completely unrelated reasons. If the "value becomes a named place" rule just asserted a single *global* place named `A` whenever *any* place anywhere held that value, then:

* `fanin` instance #1's selector holding `"A"` correctly fires its own `A`-branch — fine.
* But `fanin` instance #2, whose selector currently holds `"C"`, would *also* see place `A` become valid (because something else, somewhere, happened to assert it), and if instance #2 also has an `A`-named branch rule, it would spuriously fire too — even though instance #2's actual selector never said `A`.

That's the collision I meant: not "the same token exists twice" (harmless), but "a synthesized dispatch flag meant to be private to one invocation leaks into a namespace another, unrelated invocation also reads from."

**This is avoidable, and we already have the machinery to avoid it.** `inlineInvocation` already renames every place inside a callee with a per-invocation prefix (`fanin#0.`, `fanin#1.`, etc.) specifically so two instances of the same callee never collide. If the "value becomes a place" rule were built *as part of* that same renaming step — so the synthesized place name is `fanin#0.A` rather than a bare global `A` — the collision disappears entirely, because it inherits the exact same isolation every other place in that invocation already gets. So this isn't a fundamental blocker, just something that has to be built *inside* the existing renaming machinery, not bolted on as a separate global rule afterward. I was too quick to frame it as a blanket risk without saying that part.

**That said, there may be a cleaner fix specifically for** `fanin`/`fanout` that avoids synthesizing any place name at all. We already have a mechanism that reads *values* directly instead of relying on name-identity: `.select`, used by `AND`/`OR`/`NOT`'s `res<$A$B()>` form. It reads `env.get(input)` for each input, joins the actual values, and looks the result up in a table — no synthesized place needed, and it already works correctly inside invocation (that's exactly what makes `AND3` work today). If `$select( ) : A[out<$in1>] ...` were compiled the same way — read the actual value of `select`, match it against each branch's name as a string, run that branch's fill — the whole token-identity question goes away for this case. Smaller, more contained change, and provably safe under invocation already.

**I don't think that same fix applies cleanly to** `FULLADD`'s chaining problem, though, and I want to flag that distinction rather than let it look resolved too. `FULLADD`'s joint-match rows (`S,U,W[K,M]`) use token-identity the same way — but joint-match is the *primary* mechanism almost every other working example relies on ([TAG-177](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-177/example-1226-pure-value-expression-of-boolean-full-adder), [TAG-198](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-198/example-1225-pure-value-expression), [TAG-211](https://linear.app/taguniversal/issue/TAG-211/example-1218-bundling-digits-into-numbers), etc.), not a narrow dispatch form. Recompiling joint-match itself to be value-keyed instead of place-identity-keyed would be a much bigger, more invasive change touching most of what currently works, not something to do casually. For that case, the scoped-reification idea (still pending the book check on scope) is probably the safer path. So these two may end up needing different-sized fixes even though they share the same root cause.

Given that, I'd suggest: do the narrow `.select`-style fix for `fanin`/`fanout` now, since it's small and low-risk, and keep the broader joint-match-under-invocation question as its own separate, book-checked ticket rather than conflating the two. Want me to write the `fanin`/`fanout` fix first, or move to TAG-215's topological sort since that's unambiguous and you were about to paste the file for it?
